prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the clearest chain from hormone physiology to a transformative medicine on the shortlist: proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, the active truncated peptide and receptor biology led to drugs with large, independently confirmed effects on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. All six openings ranked it first, but I rest my support on the science, not the tally: it is original, the mechanism is settled, the clinical evidence comes from many independent outcome trials, and the field is mature enough that recognition is timely. A single-achievement prize also avoids splitting among crowded claimants. The central appetite action of GLP-1 also ties the work to neural circuit control of feeding, which I note only as a scientific link and not as a reason for preference.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Credit for identifying the active GLP-1(7-36) form is contested among Mojsov, Habener and others, and Habener is not among the credited names. Knudsen's drug-development role is decisive for the therapeutics, so a three-person physiology prize can look as if it rewards the discovery and leaves out the medicine. If the committee considers the prize incomplete without the therapeutic step, or the Mojsov priority question unresolvable, the configuration is weaker than the unanimity of the openings suggests.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked B021 first but treated the three-person physiology trio as plausible and not settled, and flagged whether drug-development credit for Knudsen is a policy question. He ranked CAR-T second and proposed June and Sadelain only.
responses.response: I agree that Knudsen is a policy question and not a scientific one. I would still keep the physiology trio, because the Nobel tradition favours the discovery that made the therapy possible, and the drug-development step builds on a hormone biology that Holst and Drucker established. I also share your view that Rosenberg's claim in CAR-T is weaker than that of June and Sadelain for the CAR-specific advance. I included him in my opening ranking only to credit adoptive cell therapy, and on reflection a June and Sadelain pair is cleaner. I do not accept that this makes CAR-T the better first choice, because the missing Eshhar credit remains.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked TNF blockade (B032) second and cGAS-STING (B015) third, calling Feldmann and Maini a clean two-person attribution with decades of confirmation, while noting her own field familiarity as a possible bias.
responses.response: The two-person TNF attribution is cleaner than anything else on the list, and I respect that you disclosed your field familiarity. I still disagree with ranking it above CAR-T or optogenetics. It is largely the clinical proof of a concept that rested on upstream TNF biology and antibody engineering outside the credited names, as Svenningsson also notes. The case is strong but is more a long-overdue clinical translation than a new principle, and I would keep it as a fallback, not a lead. On cGAS-STING, I agree with your Chen and Barber pairing as the cleanest, but with no clinical benefit shown yet the claim rests on mechanism alone, which is why I put it below the therapeutic candidates.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked optogenetics third, noting that six credited names cannot fit a three-person cap, and that the allocation between discovering channelrhodopsin and applying it in neurons is contested. He proposed Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann.
responses.response: This is my own field, so I take the allocation problem seriously. I now think my opening trio of Boyden, Deisseroth and Hegemann was too much weighted toward neuronal application. The channelrhodopsin discovery by Nagel, Hegemann and Bamberg is the molecular foundation, and your Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann split better reflects the distinction between discovery and use. Even so, leaving out Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenbock leaves genuine claims unrecognised, and a methods prize is a harder fit for the physiology or medicine remit than a therapy. That is why I keep optogenetics as an alternative and not as my preference.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked cGAS-STING out of his list and placed UPR (B052) third and the SMN2 antisense therapy (B042) fourth, arguing that Walter and Mori are a clean pair and that Krainer and Bennett support a two-person prize.
responses.response: I agree the Walter and Mori attribution is clean and that the pathway is mechanistically elegant. I rated the UPR below my top group because its direct medical translation is still indirect, and Ron, Kaufman and Kohno claims are outside the credited names. I also disagree with ranking it above optogenetics on maturity grounds, since both are mature and the latter has had wider reach. On B042 I ranked it low in my opening ranking, and I want to be fair to it: nusinersen is a striking, mechanism-driven result in a motor neuron disease. It still rests on SMN gene discovery by others, and the platform is younger, so I consider it a later candidate than the GLP-1 work.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1 peptide can be credited without Habener, and whether the supplied credited names capture it fully.
Whether the committee should reward drug development (Knudsen) alongside, or instead of, a basic-physiology laureate.
Whether a two-part prize pairing GLP-1 with CAR-T or optogenetics is warranted, given that the three-person cap would then force fewer GLP-1 names.
If optogenetics is pursued, how to allocate among the six credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict is apparent from my profile for the GLP-1 candidate. For transparency, I have co-authored with Thomas Perlmann (a 2009 stem-cell-derived dopamine neuron paper) and my field of motor-circuit neuroscience overlaps with optogenetics as a user of such tools, though I have no documented tie to any credited optogenetics candidate.
